strengths: The core question — can pathwise (reparameterized/deterministic) policy gradients be used reliably in a fully on-policy setting — is well-motivated and addresses a real gap between on-policy methods (PPO) and off-policy actor-critic methods (SAC/TD3), with clear practical relevance for GPU-parallelized RL.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 31 tasks across two GPU-parallelized benchmarks (mujoco_playground DMC and ManiSkill), multiple random seeds (10 for REPPO), rliable aggregate metrics (mean/median/IQM with 95% bootstrap CIs), and per-environment curves that honestly show failure cases (e.g., FingerSpin).

Baselines are treated fairly: the authors tuned PPO themselves for sample efficiency, and compare against FastTD3 under matched memory budgets, which directly supports the memory-footprint claims. The wall-clock comparison is also done.

The paper includes meaningful ablations (KL regularization, HL-Gauss categorical critic, layer normalization, auxiliary self-prediction loss, buffer size) that identify which components actually matter, rather than only presenting the final method.

The joint entropy/KL dual temperature tuning and forward-KL (rather than reverse-KL) trust region choice is a sensible, well-argued design contribution, and the algorithmic insights are clearly explained with detailed pseudocode and released code in both JAX and PyTorch, supporting reproducibility.
The 'reliable performance' stability metric and memory-constrained comparisons provide a useful and somewhat novel evaluation angle beyond standard final-return reporting.
weaknesses: Component-level novelty is limited: the algorithm is largely a recombination of existing techniques (TD-λ targets, SAC-style entropy temperature tuning, KL regularization à la REPS/TRPO, HL-Gauss categorical critic from Farebrother et al. 2024, layer normalization, self-predictive auxiliary tasks). The conceptual contribution is closest to PQN (Gallici et al. 2024) adapted to continuous actions; the paper positions this honestly but the delta is incremental.

There is no theoretical analysis of why the method works on-policy (e.g., bias of the pathwise gradient under an on-policy-fitted surrogate, or properties of the KL-constrained update); the contribution is entirely empirical, and the illustrative toy experiment (Figure 1) is quite simplistic.

The hyperparameter-robustness claim is weakened by the fact that the discount factor γ and HL-Gauss support (vmin/vmax) are tuned automatically per environment (Appendix D), so not everything truly transfers with 'a single hyperparameter set'.

Several presentation defects: unresolved references ('in ??' for implementation details), apparent typos in the update rules (Eq. 19 updates β using the entropy term instead of the KL term; the G^(n) index in Eq. 12 starts at k=t; Eq. 13's normalization appears inconsistent), and the ManiSkill comparison lacks an SAC-style off-policy baseline, making it harder to judge the manipulation results.

Evaluation is confined to state-based simulation benchmarks; no vision-based tasks, no real-robot transfer, and limited evidence outside locomotion/manipulation, which narrows the demonstrated scope of the claims.

The auxiliary-task component has inconsistent effects (helps in some environments, harmful in others), which the authors acknowledge but do not resolve, leaving an unresolved design element in the method.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: whether pathwise (deterministic/value-gradient) policy updates can work in a fully on-policy setting, which is a relevant and underexplored angle given the recent popularity of GPU-parallelized simulation (MPS).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 23 DMC + 8 ManiSkill tasks, aggregate metrics with 95% bootstrap CIs (Agarwal et al. style), 4–10 seeds per configuration, training curves, a 'reliable performance' stability metric, wall-clock comparisons, memory-footprint comparisons, and component ablations at two data scales.

Reasonable ablation study that honestly reports mixed effects (e.g., the auxiliary loss helps in some environments and hurts in others; KL removal drops performance below PPO), which increases credibility.
Reproducibility support: code in both jax and torch, hyperparameter table, and a candid appendix discussion of wall-clock measurement pitfalls.
Clear positioning relative to prior work (PQN, FastTD3, PQL, MPO/V-MPO, REPS) and honest acknowledgment of tasks where PPO beats the method.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: REPPO is essentially a recipe combining well-known components — SAC-style pathwise gradients, maximum-entropy RL, TD(λ)/GAE targets, HL-Gauss (Farebrother et al., 2024), layer normalization, self-predictive auxiliary losses (Schwarzer et al., 2021), and KL-constrained updates (REPS/TRPO) with SAC-style dual temperature tuning. The main contribution is an engineering integration; the paper offers no theoretical analysis of why an on-policy critic trained once per iteration suffices, nor any new estimator or objective with guarantees.

Technical writing/notation errors undermine confidence: Eq. (14) regresses on G^(n) although the method defines G^λ; the index conventions in Eq. (12) are inconsistent (sum 'from k=t to n-1' with γ^k); Eq. (19) (the β update) appears to use the entropy term H[π] where the KL term should appear — a typo in a core mechanism; Eq. (21)'s KL condition is written over a sum of log-ratios without a KL-target constant in view; a broken reference '??' remains in Section 4.1.

The core design choice of forward-KL (mode-covering) regularization is justified only informally ('our unimodal policy makes its mode-averaging behavior benign') with no analysis or experiment isolating forward vs. reverse KL, even though the paper claims this as a key insight.

Claims of 'high hyperparameter robustness' and 'a single hyperparameter set' across 30+ tasks are under-supported: no sensitivity analysis (e.g., over KL_target, H_target, λ, learning rates) is shown; γ and the HL-Gauss bin ranges are still tuned per environment, weakening the robustness claim.

Missing important baselines: no comparison to a continuous-action adaptation of PQN (the closest related work) or to TRPO/SAC-lagrangian-style variants, making it hard to attribute gains to the on-policy pathwise idea vs. the specific component stack. The FastTD3 memory-constrained comparison (32k buffer) is a somewhat artificial handicap of the off-policy baseline.
The 'reliable performance' metric (τ=0.9 threshold) is ad hoc, threshold-dependent, and results are reported only as aggregate percentages without per-task analysis or sensitivity to τ.

The illustrative toy experiment (Fig. 1) uses hand-constructed surrogate quality (32 vs. 1024 samples) and initializes near the optimum; its conclusions about MC vs. pathwise gradients are well-known and add little.

Some framing is overstated relative to evidence, e.g., 'addresses the issue at the root,' 'should lead to more trustworthy deployment of RL algorithms in the wild,' and the 33% wall-clock improvement claim rests on a single-node, single-framework (jax) comparison the authors themselves argue is fragile.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: making pathwise (first-order) policy gradients work in a fully on-policy setting, addressing a genuine gap since existing pathwise methods rely on off-policy replay buffers.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning two modern GPU-parallelized benchmarks (23 mujoco_playground DMC tasks + 8 ManiSkill tasks, 30+ environments) with multiple seeds (10 for the proposed method), aggregate metrics (mean/median/IQM) with bootstrapped confidence intervals, and evaluation along several practically relevant axes: final performance, sample efficiency, reliability of policy improvement, wall-clock time, and memory footprint.

Thoughtful comparison against a strong recent off-policy baseline (FastTD3), including a memory-constrained FastTD3 variant that isolates the memory-vs-performance tradeoff — this strengthens the claim that on-policy training is the key advantage rather than just a weaker baseline.

Useful design ablations (HL-Gauss loss, layer normalization, auxiliary self-predictive loss, KL regularization) at two data scales, with honest reporting that the auxiliary loss has inconsistent effects and that PPO wins on some environments.
Reproducibility support: implementations in both JAX and PyTorch, a hyperparameter table, a single hyperparameter set across 30+ tasks, and an appendix on the pitfalls of wall-clock measurement.
The illustrative toy experiment (Section 2.3) cleanly builds intuition about the variance/bias tradeoff between score-function and pathwise estimators.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: REPPO is largely a careful combination of existing techniques (SAC-style entropy tuning, REPS/PPO-style KL constraints, TD(λ)/GAE targets, HL-Gauss categorical critics, layer normalization, self-predictive auxiliary losses from SPR/BCQ-style works). The main contribution is an engineering recipe and the demonstration that these combine successfully on-policy, which is valuable but incremental; theoretical justification for why the on-policy surrogate Q suffices is absent.

Several technical and notational issues that should have been caught: the β update in Eq. (19) appears to copy the entropy term H[πθ(x)] instead of the KL term; the summation index in Eq. (12) starts at k=t which is inconsistent; a broken cross-reference ('We report all implementation details... in ??'); the illustrative toy experiment initializes near the global minimum, which arguably weakens the claimed failure of MC gradients.

Some methodological choices are asserted rather than validated: the preference for forward KL over reverse KL, and the claim that jointly tuning entropy and KL multipliers is 'crucial', are supported only by end-to-end performance, not by targeted analyses (e.g., plots of KL/entropy trajectories, or ablations of the joint vs. independent tuning schemes).

Baseline fairness concerns: only 4 seeds for PPO baselines and 5 for FastTD3 vs. 10 for REPPO; the tuned-PPO search scope is not fully characterized; SAC baselines are borrowed from prior benchmark papers rather than re-tuned for these settings, while PPO receives an extra hyperparameter search.

Evidence for 'hyperparameter robustness' is claimed but never rigorously demonstrated (no sensitivity curves over H_target, KL_target, λ, learning rate); the robustness claim rests on a single default set transferring across tasks, which is suggestive but not a controlled study.

Writing quality is uneven: recurring grammatical errors ('that allow training', 'achieves converges', 'competetive', 'environemnts') and minor inconsistencies reduce polish; scope is limited to continuous-action, state-observation control, so generality claims (e.g., relevance to RLHF-style LLM fine-tuning in the motivation) are not supported by experiments.
The reliability metric ('reliable performance') is self-defined with an arbitrary threshold τ = 0.9; while intuitively sensible, its novelty and statistical treatment are limited.

strengths: The core question — whether pathwise (deterministic-style) policy gradients can work in a fully on-policy setting without replay buffers — is well-motivated and clearly articulated, and the paper provides a convincing affirmative answer.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: 30+ tasks across two GPU-parallelized benchmarks (MuJoCo Playground DMC and ManiSkill), 20 seeds with bootstrapped confidence intervals and outlier-robust aggregate metrics (IQM, median), a 'reliable success' stability metric, wall-clock comparisons, and a discrete-action variant on Atari.

The ablation comparing REPPO (pathwise) vs. score-based variants with the same learned Q function and the same framework (Figure 3) is a well-designed experiment that isolates the contribution of the pathwise estimator, and the design ablations (KL, HL-Gauss, normalization, auxiliary loss at two batch sizes) support the claimed component importance.

The joint entropy/KL multiplier tuning with target constraints is a sensible and apparently important mechanism for controlling on-policy value-based updates; the ablation showing removal of the KL term drops performance below PPO supports this claim.

The memory comparison against FastTD3 with matched small buffers (two to three orders of magnitude smaller) is a fair and practically relevant control; the paper also candidly discusses wall-clock measurement pitfalls.
Code is provided in both JAX and PyTorch, and hyperparameters follow a single default set across tasks, supporting reproducibility and the hyperparameter-robustness claim.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily integrative: the method combines known ingredients (maximum-entropy objectives, KL-constrained updates from REPS/TRPO, HL-Gauss categorical critic, layer normalization, self-predictive auxiliary losses), and its relation to PQN, MPO, and Nauman & Cygan (2025) is acknowledged but the genuinely new technical insight is relatively narrow (jointly tuned entropy + KL targets in the on-policy pathwise regime).

There is essentially no theoretical analysis: the paper relies on intuition plus the toy example; the biased surrogate-based estimator, the constrained formulation (10)-(12) and its relaxation, and the clip-based enforcement in Eq. 15 are justified only empirically.

Some baselines are weakened: SAC results are taken from prior papers rather than re-tuned; RPO and DPO are dismissed after failed tuning; FastTD3 uses only 5 seeds with an admitted failure to replicate its claimed speed; the wall-clock comparison is restricted to PPO in JAX, so the efficiency claims rest on a limited comparison set.

Presentation issues suggest unfinished polish: a broken cross-reference ('??' for the HL-Gauss math), several typos ('perforamnce', 'appraoches', 'sepcific', 'environemnts'), and Eq. 13-14 / Eq. 15 notation is dense and hard to verify (e.g., the KL condition in Eq. 15 uses a sample-based ratio whose correctness is nontrivial).

The auxiliary self-predictive loss is reported as harmful in some environments and helpful in others, yet it is kept on by default with a recommendation for practitioners to investigate — this weakens the 'robustness' narrative slightly.

Evaluation is limited to GPU-parallelized simulation benchmarks (plus Atari); there is no evidence on more standard CPU-based MuJoCo/DMC settings or on transfer to harder/higher-dimensional domains where the memory claims would matter most.

strengths: The core question—whether pathwise (deterministic-style) policy gradients can work in a fully on-policy setting without replay buffers—is well-motivated and relevant to the massively parallel simulation regime where replay memory is a genuine bottleneck.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad: 23 mujoco_playground DMC tasks and 8 ManiSkill tasks, 20 seeds, aggregate metrics (mean/median/IQM) with 95% bootstrap CIs following Agarwal et al., plus a reliable-success metric for stability.

Component ablations (HL-Gauss categorical critic, KL regularization, layer normalization, auxiliary self-prediction) are provided at two data scales, and the discrete-action variant on Atari-10 adds breadth beyond continuous control.
The memory comparison against FastTD3 with a size-matched buffer (Figure 11) is a fair and informative control that supports the memory-footprint claim.
The paper is transparent about wall-clock measurement pitfalls and about the inconsistent (sometimes harmful) effect of the auxiliary task.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: REPPO is essentially an assembly of well-known components (SAC-style pathwise gradients, maximum-entropy rewards, REPS/MPO-style KL constraints with automatic multiplier tuning, HL-Gauss, layer normalization, self-predictive auxiliary losses). The methodological contribution relative to prior work such as PQN, MPO, and Nauman & Cygan (2025) is incremental, and the paper does not clearly delineate which combination insight is itself novel.

The motivating toy experiment (Section 2.2, Figure 2) is close to a strawman: the score-based baseline appears to lack standard variance reduction, and the learning rate was explicitly chosen to favor the ground-truth pathwise method (Appendix C.1), so the claimed contrast in stability is partly baked in.

There is a mismatch between the theoretical framing and the actual objective: Equation 15 clips based on a sum of log-ratios rather than the KL divergence stated in the constraint (Equation 11), and the KL/entropy constraints are relaxed into a soft Lagrangian with clipping—so the 'principled constrained optimization' story oversells what is implemented. No analysis is given of when the KL constraint is actually maintained.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: the 'single hyperparameter set' robustness claim is softened by per-environment tuning of gamma and HL-Gauss ranges (Table 2 / Appendix C.2), and the auxiliary task is admitted to be harmful in some environments with no principled criterion for when to use it.

Wall-clock comparisons are only against their own JAX PPO; FastTD3 is excluded from Figure 6 on framework grounds, so the 'superior wall-clock efficiency' claim rests on a limited and somewhat self-serving comparison.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a top venue: a broken cross-reference ('Subsection ??'), an incomplete sentence ('Our code is available a'), multiple typos ('constrained is currently violated', 'perforamnce', 'appraoches', 'competetive', 'environemnts'), and duplicated Chan et al. 2020a/2020b references for the same paper.

The PPO baseline, while reasonable, may understate what a heavily tuned modern PPO (e.g., with observed normalization, value clipping, and better schedules) achieves; the paper's framing that score-based methods are inherently unstable would benefit from stronger baselines.

strengths: Addresses a clear and relevant research question: whether pathwise (deterministic-style) policy gradients can be made to work in a fully on-policy setting without replay buffers. The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and the paper convincingly demonstrates its viability.

Very thorough empirical evaluation: 30+ tasks across three benchmarks (mujoco_playground DMC, ManiSkill3, Atari-10), 20 seeds for main comparisons, IQM/median/mean aggregates with 95% bootstrapped CIs following Agarwal et al. (2021), per-environment curves, and reliability metrics.

Good ablation coverage: the contribution of each component (HL-Gauss categorical critic, KL regularization, layer norm, auxiliary self-prediction) is isolated at two data scales, and the memory comparison against FastTD3 with a matched small buffer is a thoughtful and honest control.

Strong practical positioning: a single hyperparameter set across 30+ tasks, implementations in both JAX and PyTorch, an honest appendix discussing the pitfalls of wall-clock comparisons, and a discrete-action variant.

The KL/entropy dual-multiplier tuning scheme (Eq. 13-14) with the clipped actor objective is a sensible, practically motivated design, and the ablation showing KL regularization is the single critical component is a useful insight.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the algorithm is largely a recombination of existing techniques (SAC-style entropy temperature tuning, REPS/MPO-style KL constraints, TD-lambda, HL-Gauss, layer norm, self-predictive auxiliaries) applied in an on-policy regime. The paper's contribution is empirical integration rather than a new principle.

Missing analysis of the key technical risk: within an iteration, the actor is updated for multiple epochs against a critic trained on behavior-policy data, so the Q values used for the pathwise gradient become off-policy/stale. The paper never quantifies this bias or explains theoretically why the KL constraint is sufficient to keep it bounded; the clipped objective in Eq. 15 (triggering on a mean log-ratio statistic) appears ad hoc and is not derived from the stated constrained optimization problem.

Some central comparisons rely on baseline numbers reported by other papers (Brax PPO/SAC, ManiSkill PPO) rather than re-tuned baselines under identical conditions, and FastTD3 uses only 5 seeds on smaller GPUs than the authors' own hardware, which could understate the strongest competitor. RPO and DPO 'could not be tuned above PPO,' which suggests possible baseline-under-tuning.
Wall-clock claims are only made against PPO in JAX; a direct head-to-head with FastTD3 (the main off-policy competitor) is explicitly omitted, weakening the efficiency claims.

Presentation issues that should not appear at this stage: a broken cross-reference ('We present the mathematical form of the loss formulation in ??'), multiple typos ('constrained is currently violated', 'perforamnce', 'sepcific', 'environemnts'), and Figure 2's toy experiment uses surrogate models trained on the objective itself, which only weakly transfers to the MDP setting.

The auxiliary-task component is admitted to be inconsistently helpful (harmful in some environments), and the paper's guidance for when to use it is essentially 'practitioners should investigate' -- an unresolved design question within the method.
